title: Security Operations Bulletin
content:
Security Operations Bulletin
Report date: 2026-08-02
Severity: High
Category: Phishing / Credential Theft
Scope: Users accessing email, cloud apps, and internal portals

Executive Summary
A phishing campaign is currently targeting users with fake login prompts that imitate trusted services. If a user enters credentials on the fake page, attackers may gain access to email, files, and connected business systems. The primary risk is account compromise, followed by data exposure and unauthorized message sending from the victim’s account.

Incident Details
What is happening:
Users receive urgent messages asking them to verify accounts, reset passwords, or review a shared document. These messages often contain links to lookalike sign-in pages designed to capture usernames, passwords, and MFA codes.

Who is affected:
Any user who interacts with the message, especially those with access to email, cloud storage, finance systems, or administrative tools.

Impact:

Account takeover.

Unauthorized access to mailboxes and files.

Possible lateral movement into internal systems.

Business email compromise or fraud attempts.

Indicators to Watch
Unexpected login prompts or MFA requests.

Emails with urgency, threats, or password-expiry language.

Suspicious domains that resemble legitimate services.

Unusual sign-in alerts from unfamiliar locations or devices.

Containment Actions
Block or quarantine the phishing message across mail channels.

Force password reset for any user who submitted credentials.

Review sign-in logs for anomalous access and impossible travel.

Revoke active sessions and tokens for affected accounts.

Alert users to report similar emails immediately.

User Guidance
Users should not click links or open attachments from suspicious messages. They should verify requests through a trusted channel, report suspicious emails to security, and change passwords immediately if they suspect exposure.

Escalation Status
This event should be escalated if any user credentials were entered, MFA prompts were approved unexpectedly, or suspicious sign-ins are detected in account logs.

content: THREAT BULLETIN: Black Basta RansomwareDate: July 22, 2026Threat Actor: Black Basta Operators / AffiliatesThreat Type: Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS)Target Sectors: Global Critical Infrastructure, Healthcare, Manufacturing, and Enterprise NetworksExecutive SummaryBlack Basta is a highly active Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) platform written in C++. In development since February 2022 and deployed in the field since April 2022, the group utilizes a aggressive double-extortion model. Affiliates encrypt operational data and simultaneously exfiltrate sensitive information, leveraging the threat of public data leaks to force cryptocurrency payments.Technical Profile & Tactics1. Initial Access & Lateral MovementInitial Vectors: Exploitation of known vulnerabilities (e.g., ConnectWise, Fortinet), malicious phishing campaigns (Qakbot, DarkGate), and compromised Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) credentials.Reconnaissance: Deploys tools like SoftPerfect Network Scanner and Advanced IP Scanner to map corporate environments.Lateral Movement: Utilizes native administrative tools (Living off the Land) such as PsExec, Remote Desktop, and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).2. Evasion & Defense DisruptionSecurity Disabling: Terminates Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents, antivirus software, and Windows Defender services prior to payload execution.Shadow Copy Deletion: Executes PowerShell and vssadmin commands to wipe volume shadow copies, preventing local system recovery.Safe Mode Booting: Configures compromised systems to boot into Safe Mode with Networking to bypass active security monitoring tools during encryption.3. Data Exfiltration & EncryptionExfiltration: Uses tools like Rclone to upload vast amounts of corporate data to cloud storage providers (e.g., Mega) before launching encryption.Encryption Engine: Implements a fast, multi-threaded C++ encryption routine targeting local drives, network shares, and VMware ESXi environments.Extortion: Appends a randomized extension to encrypted files and drops a readme.txt ransom note detailing communication instructions via a Tor negotiation portal.

title: TanStack npm packages compromised: inside the Mini Shai-Hulud supply chain attack
content:
TanStack npm packages compromised: inside the Mini Shai-Hulud supply chain attack
On May 11, 2026, between 19:20 and 19:26 UTC, 84 malicious npm package artifacts were published across 42 packages in the @tanstack namespace. The packages were not published by an attacker who stole credentials; they were published by TanStack's legitimate release pipeline, using its trusted OIDC identity, after attacker-controlled code hijacked the runner mid-workflow. The malicious versions spread to Mistral AI, UiPath, and dozens of other maintainers within hours. @tanstack/react-router alone receives over 12.7 million weekly downloads (npm API).

The incident is attributed by StepSecurity to the threat group known as TeamPCP, and it is also the first documented case of a malicious npm package carrying valid SLSA provenance. SLSA provenance is a cryptographic certificate, generated by Sigstore, that is meant to verify a package was built from a trusted source. The worm was able to produce these certificates because it hijacked the legitimate build pipeline itself; Sigstore verified the build process correctly. What SLSA does not guarantee is that the code being built was safe.

If your team installed any affected @tanstack/* version on May 11, treat the install environment as compromised and rotate every secret accessible from that host. Keep reading for the full package list, technical breakdown, and step-by-step remediation.

The malicious versions spread to Mistral AI, UiPath, and dozens of other maintainers within hours. @tanstack/react-router alone receives over 12.7 million weekly downloads (npm API).

The incident is attributed by StepSecurity to the threat group known as TeamPCP, and it is also the first documented case of a malicious npm package carrying valid SLSA provenance. SLSA provenance is a cryptographic certificate, generated by Sigstore, that is meant to verify a package was built from a trusted source. The worm was able to produce these certificates because it hijacked the legitimate build pipeline itself; Sigstore verified the build process correctly. What SLSA does not guarantee is that the code being built was safe.

If your team installed any affected @tanstack/* version on May 11, treat the install environment as compromised and rotate every secret accessible from that host. Keep reading for the full package list, technical breakdown, and step-by-step remediation.
